title: Challenges with Agentic game development?
author: National-County6310
selftext:
I have been doing agentic game development for a while. But I sometimes i struggle and I wounder if it's me? Some tasks are just so complex using agents some are simpler.   
I don't talk about small vibe coded projects I mean full games. 

  
What is your major challenge's or recent challenges you have solved?

comments.author: fissionchips303
comments.body:
The hardest thing for me coming from a web and mobile background is just biting off more than I can chew. I have made two projects 90% by hand and 10% vibe coded, neither released, but I would say both having a decent chance of being an actual game if I had the time and energy. One is a point and click adventure where anywhere you click, your dude walks around with a nice walking animation. I spent weeks just getting about 40 or 50 screens made and polishing it all. It’s in unity, all 3d, fixed camera view, sometimes zoomed in sometimes farther out. Your guy is a really nice free 3d asset I found. He just walks wherever you click and has great pathing to get up hills and around obstacles and whatnot. I spent tons of time putting in ambient sound effects that are unique to each area. I guess I was inspired by Myst and old point and clicks like Sierra games, Lucasarts etc.

So that one I feel good about even though I never finished it, I did start programming convos with npcs, ability to pick up items, inventory etc. it just feels good and actually has atmosphere and vibe.

Second one I feel good about is inspired by old LPmud. Same thing, fixed camera on 3d landscapes, this time no character avatar and just ability to go “n” “ne” “e” etc and navigate, and in each area to select from various commands to do. 

These are 2 of like 20 games I tried making and those 2 ended up getting the farthest because they actually have polished enjoyable atmosphere, ambient sound effects, “vibe” (not in the sense of vibe coded, just the gameworld itself has vibe). In both cases AI helped me figure stuff out but it was mostly querying and just a little bit of coding.

Compare this to when I work in web and now literally 95% of the code I write comes from augment. 

I wish I could use AI more for game dev, I just do so much visually in unity and when I do write c# I just ask AI questions or to help me write little things rather than create or edit files directly. Though I want to learn! I heard there is a good unity plugin if anyone has tools they want to share here. But yeah my only advice (as someone who has never released a game, so take it with a grain of salt) is to design features you can realistically build. My two favorite forays into games each have something I was able to build and polish to the point it starts feeling really fun to just exist in the game world and navigate around. But again those are for specific kinds of games (point and click adventure, screen based rpg)

replies.author: National-County6310
replies.body: Interesting. Yes I agree main problem is spatial understanding. Less UI and AI performs better. ;)

comments.author: _DRZS
comments.body: The biggest challenge for me is the context loss. I found it helps to have a clear vision and roadmap that you can plug it into your agent's knowledge base so you both have a source of truth

comments.author: alphapussycat
comments.body: You wouldn't use agentic AI for anything beyond something isolated.

replies.author: National-County6310
replies.body: How do you mean and why? I’m curious to understand your thinking…

replies.author: alphapussycat
replies.body:
It's not gonna code anything right, and I imagine the costs will be astronomical.

I use AI to brainstorm with, or code pieces of code to specification.

As some AI leader dev said. Humans are capable of end-end problem solving, while AI can really only do middle-middle. The human still need to get an understanding of the problem, use AI to help with the middle work, and then the human has to confirm and implement.

AI code is hard to read, and you'll be doing a ton of AI code reading if you have to manually approve every single thing.

replies.author: vaksninus
replies.body: You don't really need to read it if you understand the desired input, output, common edge cases and somewhat typical design approach so you know the solution isn't too weird, honestly you think you code better than claude code and that the minute coding details matter? Manually coding is a waste of time

replies.author: alphapussycat
replies.body:
Claude and perplexity are good at some parts of coding. However, they don't understand how to code for performance. e.g. They'll often opt for things like hashmaps.

e.g. if you make game in unity, they will not create custom memory stuff, or write with "unsafe code".

You'll have very low performance if you let Claude code everything. You must tell it what it's allowed to use, what it should use etc. If you hand hold all the details it can probably code it, but those will be as large prompt as you'd have to code yourself.

It's really only valuable to have it as finding typos, and handling compile error logs. And generally giving you tips on coding, or map out some coding pattern etc.

replies.author: National-County6310
replies.body: That  interesting takes as you both see it quite differently. I think guidelines are important. But some times it’s so bad and some times crazy good. I use a lot of test but for complex code across multiple fillies and components and game objects oh my it fail so hard… I believe it’s possible to do a lot more but I’m not there yet.

replies.author: alphapussycat
replies.body:
I made a game engine recently, and I one wrapper had multiple templates of templates. I had essentially 4 functions, but because of all the permutations I had to code 56 functions to cover all bases... I think AI could've done it... But I would still had to read through it... And most work was just copy paste and changing a few things.

So that's a good use case, but I think trust on AI is still too low. It could always mess up, so I feel like one always have to proof read.

But it helped me immensely when it mapped out a registry and factory, and macros to handle it, to make it easy to create new things in code and seeing them in the editor.

Atm, I think I use it more as a learning, helper and correctioning tool, rather than something that actually produces code.

replies.author: National-County6310
replies.body: That trust is so important. I use test for trust and documented code for trust but most of all watch the intent of the first plan. Still run in to problem tough. :) I guess its part of learning. Thanks for sharing!

comments.author: Big-Passenger-4723
comments.body: It is always the verification part for me. I spent over 50% of my time just to verify what AI agents wrote.

replies.author: National-County6310
replies.body: Ahh yes. That is the complex part I think too. It doesn’t understand the tests….

comments.author: build_logic
comments.body: From what I have seen, the main friction tends to appear once the project grows beyond isolated tasks. Agents can help generate pieces of logic or boilerplate, but maintaining consistency across systems becomes harder. Things like context loss, verification, and integration with the rest of the codebase usually take more time than expected. It often works best when the agents are used for small contained problems rather than full system design.

replies.author: National-County6310
replies.body: So how do you combat that?

replies.author: AvengerDr
replies.body: Get a degree in Computer Science? This also applies to people who improvised themselves as "developers" after watching YouTube tutorials, not just vibe coders.

replies.author: National-County6310
replies.body: I agree in part but it's also a specific problem to Game development as it's not pure code but multiple layers and user experience in 3D... I do VR dev and that is even worse :). It's so hard for AI to grasp the concepts. I turn things in to systems and modules. but still the spatial and composition of prefabs, scenes and code makes it REALY hard for AI to grasp.

comments.author: KathyJScott
comments.body: yeah the verification loop is probably the biggest challenge for me too. generating code is fast but checking that it actually fits the rest of the project takes time. once a project gets larger the context problem shows up pretty quickly. I usually end up using agents for smaller pieces instead of letting them touch big systems.

replies.author: National-County6310
replies.body: Are you using tests for your game logic?

comments.author: softladdd
comments.body:
The more preparation you do with an agent BEFORE development (ie. setting up .agent an agent-owned directory, agent rulesets, personas, etc) the easier it will be down the line. Much better than just jumping in.  
Try and create as much context of your idea as possible by splitting up different workloads into tickets (which can be stored inside .agent too)

I'm playing around with agents to develop some complex game setups, and I have found this to be a lifesaver for productivity.

replies.author: National-County6310
replies.body: I agree. I try to structure around workflows and structures. Pretty much define the classes. But the problem for me is mostly when we get to the scene and components and prefabs and dynamic instantiations. Oh my. AI is so bad at that... Especially in multiplayer VR. :)

replies.author: softladdd
replies.body: I haven't used Unity MCP or anything like that, but what works for me is giving the agents full ownership over the back-end, using ScriptableObjects as a sort of config file to make little tweaks. While I work on the front-end and put everything togther and wiring up all of the agent-made scripts in scenes :)

replies.author: National-County6310
replies.body: I have never worked with scriptable objects. I know what they are but never figured out when I would want to use one really.. More that state holders for e.g. game modes that I want to set pre game start....
